title: The Fool Says There Is No God
summary: The psalm describes the fool who says in his heart that there is no God, and then widens the view: the LORD looks down from heaven and finds that all have turned away and become corrupt. Evildoers devour God's people like bread, yet they will be overwhelmed with dread, because God stands with the righteous and is the refuge of the poor. It closes with a longing for Israel's salvation to come from Zion.
story: Psalm 14 widens the concerns of the previous psalms. Psalms 10 and 12 described the wicked and the lying generation; Psalm 14 traces their behavior to its root, the practical denial of God, and then says something harder: the corruption is universal. The LORD searches for anyone who understands and seeks him and finds none. Yet the psalm does not end in despair. God is present with the righteous and is the shelter of the oppressed, and the final verse looks forward to a restoration of the whole people. The reader is being prepared to ask what kind of person can dwell with God, which is exactly the question Psalm 15 asks.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and directs it to the choirmaster. The same psalm appears again, with small differences, as Psalm 53. The most noticeable difference is the name of God: Psalm 14 uses the covenant name the LORD (Yahweh) in several places, while Psalm 53 uses God (Elohim) throughout. Psalm 53 belongs to Psalms 42 to 83, a section scholars call the Elohistic Psalter because it strongly prefers the name Elohim, probably reflecting an editorial stage in the Psalter's formation. Psalm 53 also rewrites verses 5 and 6 of Psalm 14. The existence of two versions shows that psalms were used, adapted, and collected in different settings before the book took its final shape.

Verse 7 speaks of the LORD restoring his captive people. Many scholars take that line as coming from the time of the Babylonian exile or after it (the exile began with deportations in 597 and 587 or 586 BC), perhaps added when the psalm was adapted for later worship. Others note that the Hebrew idiom can mean restoring fortunes in general, not only bringing back captives, and so could fit an earlier period of distress.
cultural:
The fool in Hebrew wisdom is not someone of low intelligence but someone morally and spiritually senseless, who lives without regard for God and neighbor. Abigail's husband in 1 Samuel 25 is named Nabal, the same word, and she says of him that his name fits him. When the fool says “There is no God”, he is not making a philosophical argument; outright atheism was rare in the ancient world. He means that God is absent, unconcerned, or irrelevant, so there will be no reckoning. The psalm immediately connects that belief to corrupt and vile deeds.

The image of God looking down from heaven to see recalls Genesis 6:5 and 11:5, where the LORD sees human wickedness before the flood and comes down to see the tower of Babel. Verse 4's image of evildoers who “devour my people like bread” pictures exploitation as casual and daily, as ordinary as eating a meal. Zion, in verse 7, is the hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood, and by extension the city as the place of God's presence and rule.
literary: Psalm 14 blends wisdom reflection with prophetic accusation and communal lament. Verse 1 states the fool's creed and its results. Verses 2 and 3 describe God's search from heaven and its verdict, with the repeated line “there is no one who does good”. Verses 4 to 6 turn to God's people and their oppressors, promising that the oppressors will be terrified by God's presence among the righteous. Verse 7 closes with a prayer for salvation. The structure moves from the general (all humanity) to the particular (God's people and their enemies) to the hopeful (Israel restored). The contrast between the fool who says “There is no God” and the LORD who is “in the company of the righteous” holds the psalm together.

outline.t: God looks down: no one does good
The oppressors and the God who shelters the poor
A longing for salvation from Zion

doctrines.note: The psalm says that corruption is not limited to a few notorious evildoers: “All have turned away”. Paul uses this to teach that all humanity stands in need of God's grace.
The workers of iniquity think there is no God, but they will be overwhelmed with dread when they discover that God is present with the people they oppress.
The closing verse longs for salvation to come from Zion and for God to restore his people. The hope of the psalm lies not in human goodness, which has failed, but in God's action.

words.note: Naval, fool. In the Old Testament the word describes someone who is morally foolish, godless, and destructive, not merely unintelligent. Nabal in 1 Samuel 25 embodies the type: churlish, ungrateful, and blind to danger. The fool's problem in verse 1 is located in the heart, the seat of will and choice, not in the mind alone.

Shachat, to ruin or corrupt. It is the verb used in Genesis 6:11-12 for the corruption of the earth before the flood. Its use in verse 1 links the fool's world with that earlier moment, when God looked on a humanity that had ruined its way.

Shevut, captivity or fortunes. The phrase in verse 7 can mean to bring back captives or, more broadly, to restore someone's fortunes. It became a key phrase in the prophets for God's promised restoration of Israel after exile (Jeremiah 29:14; Amos 9:14).

christ: Paul quotes verses 1 to 3 in Romans 3:10-12, drawing also on Psalm 53, as the opening of his case that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). He uses the psalm to show that no one, Jew or Gentile, can stand before God on their own righteousness, and then announces the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. The psalm's longing that salvation would come from Zion is answered, in the New Testament's reading, by the Messiah who came to Jerusalem, died there, and rose again. The link between verse 7 and Christ is one of hope fulfilled rather than direct prediction, but Paul's use of verses 1 to 3 is explicit.

hard.q: Is the psalm calling all atheists fools?
hard.a: The fool of Psalm 14 is not a thoughtful unbeliever wrestling with questions. In the Old Testament's vocabulary, the fool is a person who lives as though God will never call him to account, and the psalm immediately links that stance to exploitation of the poor. Its target is practical godlessness, which believers can fall into as easily as unbelievers. Paul's use of the psalm in Romans 3 underlines this: he applies verses 1 to 3 to everyone, including religious people, to show that all have turned aside. The psalm is less an insult aimed at outsiders than a mirror held up to every reader.

questions: The fool says “There is no God” in his heart, not only with his lips. Where might your daily choices say the same thing, even if your beliefs do not?
Paul uses this psalm to show that all people need grace. How does that change the way you think about those you consider wicked?
Verse 6 says the LORD is the shelter of the oppressed. How can your community reflect that shelter for people who are being exploited?
